verses.zh: 耶和华的话临到耶利米说：
verses.en: The Lord said to Jeremiah:[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying:” This same formula occurs ten other times in Jeremiah. It has already occurred at 7:1 and 11:1.

verses.zh: 「你起来，下到窑匠的家里去，我在那里要使你听我的话。」
verses.en: “Go down at once[NOTE:1] to the potter’s house. I will speak to you further there.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Get up and go down.” The first verb is not literal but is idiomatic for the initiation of an action. See 13:4, 6 for other occurrences of this idiom.
Heb “And I will cause you to hear my word there.”

verses.zh: 我就下到窑匠的家里去，正遇他转轮做器皿。
verses.en: So I went down to the potter’s house and found him working[NOTE:1] at his wheel.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “And behold he was working.”

At his wheel (Heb “at the two stones”). The Hebrew expression is very descriptive of the construction of a potter’s wheel, which consisted of two stones joined by a horizontal shaft. The potter rotated the wheel with his feet on the lower wheel and worked the clay with his hands on the upper. For a picture of a potter working at his wheel, see I. Ben-Dor, “Potter’s Wheel,” IDB 3:846. See also the discussion regarding the making of pottery in J. L. Kelso, “Pottery,” IDB 3:846-53.

verses.zh: 窑匠用泥做的器皿，在他手中做坏了，他又用这泥另做别的器皿；窑匠看怎样好，就怎样做。
verses.en: Now and then[NOTE:1] there would be something wrong[NOTE:2] with the pot he was molding from the clay[NOTE:3] with his hands. So he would rework[NOTE:4] the clay into another kind of pot as he saw fit.[NOTE:5]
notes: The verbs here denote repeated action. They are the Hebrew perfect with the vav (ו) consecutive. The text then reads somewhat literally, “Whenever the vessel he was molding…was ruined, he would remold…” For this construction see Joüon 2:393-94 §118.n and 2:628-29 §167.b, and compare the usage in Amos 4:7-8.

Something was wrong with the clay—either there was a lump in it, or it was too moist or not moist enough, or it had some other imperfection. In any case the vessel was “ruined” or “spoiled,” or defective in the eyes of the potter. This same verb has been used of the linen shorts that were “ruined” and hence “good for nothing” (Jer 13:7). The nature of the clay and how it responded to the potter’s hand determined the kind of vessel that he made of it. He did not throw the clay away. This is the basis for the application in vv. 7-10 to any nation and to the nation of Israel in particular (vv. 11-17).

The usage of the preposition בּ (bet) to introduce the material from which something is made in Exod 38:8 and 1 Kgs 15:22 should lay to rest the rather forced construction that some (like J. Bright, Jeremiah [AB], 121) put on the variant כַּחֹמֶר (kakhomer) found in a few Hebrew mss. Bright renders that phrase as an elliptical “as clay sometimes will.” The phrase is missing from the Greek version.

Heb “he would turn and work.” This is an example of hendiadys where one of the two verbs joined by “and” becomes the adverbial modifier of the other. The verb “turn” is very common in this construction (see BDB 998 s.v. שׁוּב Qal.8 for references).
Heb “as it was right in his eyes to do [or work it].” For this idiom see Judg 14:3, 7; 1 Sam 18:20, 26; 2 Sam 17:4.

verses.zh: 耶和华的话就临到我说：
verses.en: Then the Lord’s message came to me,

verses.zh: 耶和华说：「以色列家啊，我待你们，岂不能照这窑匠弄泥吗？以色列家啊，泥在窑匠的手中怎样，你们在我的手中也怎样。
verses.en: “I, the Lord, say:[NOTE:1] ‘O nation of Israel, can I not deal with you as this potter deals with the clay?[NOTE:2] In my hands, you, O nation of Israel, are just like the clay in this potter’s hand.’
notes: This phrase (literally “Oracle of the Lord”) has been handled this way on several occasions when it occurs within first person addresses where the Lord is the speaker. See, e.g., 16:16 and 17:24.
The words “deals with the clay” are not in the text. They are part of an elliptical comparison and are supplied in the translation here for clarity.

verses.zh: 我何时论到一邦或一国说，要拔出、拆毁、毁坏；
verses.en: There are times, Jeremiah,[NOTE:1] when I threaten to uproot, tear down, and destroy a nation or kingdom.[NOTE:2]
notes: The word “Jeremiah” is not in the text, but it is implicit from the introduction in v. 5 that he is being addressed. It is important to see how the rhetoric of this passage is structured. The words of vv. 7-10 lead up to the conclusion “So now” in v. 11, which in turn leads to the conclusion “Therefore” in v. 13. The tense of the verb in v. 12 is very important. It is a vav consecutive perfect indicating the future (cf. GKC 333 §112.p, r); their response is predictable. The words of vv. 7-10 are addressed to Jeremiah (v. 5) in fulfillment of the Lord’s promise to speak to him (v. 2). They furnish the basis for the Lord’s words of conditional threat to a people who show no promise of responding positively (vv. 11-12). Verse 6 then must be seen as another example of the figure of apostrophe (the turning aside from description about someone to addressing them directly; cf., e.g., Ps 6:8-9 (6:9-10 HT). Earlier examples of this figure have been seen in 6:20; 9:4; 11:13; 12:13; and 15:6.

Heb “One moment I may speak about a nation or kingdom to…” So also in v. 9. The translation is structured this way to avoid an awkward English construction and to reflect the difference in disposition. The constructions are, however, the same.

verses.zh: 我所说的那一邦，若是转意离开他们的恶，我就必后悔，不将我想要施行的灾祸降与他们。
verses.en: But if that nation I threatened stops doing wrong,[NOTE:1] I will cancel the destruction[NOTE:2] I intended to do to it.
notes: Heb “turns from its wickedness.”

There is a wordplay here involving the word “evil” (רָעָה, raʿah), which refers to both the crime and the punishment. This same play is carried further in Jonah 3:10-4:1, where Jonah becomes very displeased (Heb “it was very evil to Jonah with great evil”) when God forgoes bringing disaster (evil) on Nineveh because they have repented of their wickedness (evil).tn There is a good deal of debate about how the word translated here “revoke” should be translated. There is a good deal of reluctance to translate it “change my mind” because some see that as contradicting Num 23:19 and thus prefer “relent.” However, the English word “relent” suggests the softening of an attitude but not necessarily the change of course. It is clear that in many cases (including here) an actual change of course is in view (see, e.g., Amos 7:3, 6; Jonah 3:9; Jer 26:19; Exod 13:17; 32:14). Several of these passages deal with “conditional” prophecies, where a change in behavior of the people or the mediation of a prophet involves the change in course of the threatened punishment (or the promised benefit). “Revoke” or “forgo” may be the best way to render this in contemporary English idiom.

verses.zh: 我何时论到一邦或一国说，要建立、栽植；
verses.en: And there are times when I promise to build up and establish[NOTE:1] a nation or kingdom.
notes: Heb “plant.” The terms “uproot,” “tear down,” “destroy,” “build,” and “plant” are the two sides of the ministry Jeremiah was called to fulfill (cf. Jer 1:10).

verses.zh: 他们若行我眼中看为恶的事，不听从我的话，我就必后悔，不将我所说的福气赐给他们。
verses.en: But if that nation does what displeases me and does not obey me, then I will cancel the good I promised to do to it.

verses.zh: 现在你要对犹大人和耶路撒冷的居民说：『耶和华如此说：我造出灾祸攻击你们，定意刑罚你们。你们各人当回头离开所行的恶道，改正你们的行动作为。』
verses.en: So now, tell the people of Judah and the citizens of Jerusalem[NOTE:1] this: The Lord says, ‘I am preparing to bring disaster on you! I am making plans to punish you.[NOTE:2] So, every one of you, stop the evil things you have been doing.[NOTE:3] Correct the way you have been living and do what is right.’[NOTE:4]
notes: For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.

Heb “I am forming disaster and making plans against you.” The word translated “forming” is the same as that for “potter,” so there is a wordplay taking the reader back to v. 5. They are in his hands like the clay in the hands of the potter. Since they have not been pliable he forms new plans. He still offers them opportunity to repent, but their response is predictable.
Heb “Turn, each one from his wicked way.” See v. 8.
Or “Make good your ways and your actions.” See the same expression in 7:3, 5.

verses.zh: 「他们却说：『这是枉然。我们要照自己的计谋去行。』各人随自己顽梗的恶心做事。」
verses.en: But they just keep saying, ‘We do not care what you say![NOTE:1] We will do whatever we want to do! We will continue to behave wickedly and stubbornly!’”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “It is useless!” See the same expression in a similar context in Jer 2:25.
Heb “We will follow our own plans and do each one according to the stubbornness of his own wicked heart.”sn This has been the consistent pattern of their behavior. See 7:24; 9:13; 13:10; 16:12.

verses.zh: 所以，耶和华如此说：你们且往各国访问，有谁听见这样的事？以色列民（原文是处女）行了一件极可憎恶的事。
verses.en: Therefore, the Lord says,“Ask the people of other nationswhether they have heard of anything like this.Israel should have been like a virgin,but she has done something utterly revolting!

verses.zh: 黎巴嫩的雪从田野的磐石上岂能断绝呢？从远处流下的凉水岂能干涸呢？
verses.en: Does the snow ever completely vanish from the rocky slopes of Lebanon?Do the cool waters from those distant mountains ever cease to flow?[NOTE:1]
notes: Israel’s actions are contrary to nature. See the same kind of argumentation in Jer 2:11 and 8:7.tn The precise translation of this verse is somewhat uncertain. Two phrases in this verse are the primary cause of discussion and the source of numerous emendations, none of which has gained consensus. The phrase that is rendered here “rocky slopes” is in Hebrew צוּר שָׂדַי (tsur saday), which would normally mean something like “rocky crag of the field” (see BDB 961 s.v. שָׂדַי 1.g). Numerous emendations have been proposed, most of which are listed in the footnotes of J. A. Thompson, Jeremiah (NICOT), 436. The present translation has chosen to follow the proposal of several scholars that the word here is related to the Akkadian word shadu, meaning mountain. The other difficulty is the word translated “cease,” which in the MT is literally “be uprooted” (יִנָּתְשׁוּ, yinnateshu). The word is usually emended to read יִנָּשְׁתוּ (yinnashetu, “are dried up”) as a case of transposed letters (cf., e.g., BDB 684 s.v. נָתַשׁ Niph). This is probably a case of an error in hearing, and the word נָטַשׁ (natash), which is often parallel to עָזַב (ʿazav), translated here “vanish,” should be read in the sense that it has in 1 Sam 10:2. If one reads “are plucked up” and understands it figuratively of ceasing (“are dried” or “cease”), the sense is the same. For the sense of “distant” for the word זָרִים (zarim), see 2 Kgs 19:24.

verses.zh: 我的百姓竟忘记我，向假神烧香，使他们在所行的路上，在古道上绊跌，使他们行没有修筑的斜路，
verses.en: Yet my people have forgotten meand offered sacrifices to worthless idols.This makes them stumble along in the way they liveand leave the old reliable path of their fathers.[NOTE:1] They have left them to walk in bypaths,in roads that are not smooth and level.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “the ancient path.” This has already been referred to in Jer 6:16. There is another “old way,” but it is the path trod by the wicked (cf. Job 22:15).

Heb “ways that are not built up.” This refers to the built-up highways. See Isa 40:4 for the figure. The terms “way,” “by-paths,” and “roads” are, of course, being used here in the sense of moral behavior or action.

verses.zh: 以致他们的地令人惊骇，常常嗤笑；凡经过这地的必惊骇摇头。
verses.en: So their land will become an object of horror.[NOTE:1] People will forever hiss out their scorn over it.All who pass that way will be filled with horrorand will shake their heads in derision.[NOTE:2]
notes: There may be a deliberate double meaning involved here. The word translated “an object of horror” refers both to destruction (cf. 2:15; 4:17) and the horror or dismay that accompanies it (cf. 5:30; 8:21). The fact that there is no conjunction or preposition in front of the noun “hissing” that follows this word suggests that the reaction is in view here, not its cause. So does “be filled with horror,” which translates an etymologically related verb.

Heb “an object of lasting hissing. All who pass that way will be appalled and shake their head.”sn The actions of “shaking of the head” and “hissing” were obviously gestures of scorn and derision. See Lam 2:15-16.

verses.zh: 我必在仇敌面前分散他们，好像用东风吹散一样。遭难的日子，我必以背向他们，不以面向他们。
verses.en: I will scatter them before their enemieslike dust blowing in front of a burning east wind.I will turn my back on them and not look favorably on them[NOTE:1] when disaster strikes them.”
notes: To “turn the back” is universally recognized as a symbol of rejection. The turning of the face toward one is the subject of the beautiful Aaronic blessing in Num 6:24-26.tc Heb “I will show them [my] back and not [my] face.” This reading follows the suggestion of some of the versions and some of the Masoretes. The MT reads, “I will look on their back and not on their faces.”

verses.zh: 他们就说：「来吧！我们可以设计谋害耶利米；因为我们有祭司讲律法，智慧人设谋略，先知说预言，都不能断绝。来吧！我们可以用舌头击打他，不要理会他的一切话。」
verses.en: Then some people[NOTE:1] said, “Come on! Let us consider how to deal with Jeremiah![NOTE:2] There will still be priests to instruct us, wise men to give us advice, and prophets to declare God’s word.[NOTE:3] Come on! Let’s bring charges against him and get rid of him![NOTE:4] Then we will not need to pay attention to anything he says.”
notes: Heb “They.” The referent is unidentified; “some people” has been used in the translation.
Heb “Let us make plans against Jeremiah.” See 18:18, where this has sinister overtones as it does here.

Heb “For instruction will not perish from priest, nor counsel from wise man, nor word from prophet.”sn These are the three channels through whom God spoke to his people in the OT. See Jer 8:8-10 and Ezek 7:26.
Heb “Let us smite him with our tongues.” It is clear from the context that this involved plots to kill him.

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，求你理会我，且听那些与我争竞之人的话。
verses.en: Then I said,[NOTE:1] “Lord, pay attention to me.Listen to what my enemies are saying.[NOTE:2]
notes: The words “Then I said” are not in the text. They are supplied in the translation for clarity to show that Jeremiah turns from describing the peoples’ plots to imploring God to deal with the plotters.

Heb “the voice of my adversaries.”sn Jeremiah’s prayers against the unjust treatment of his enemies here and elsewhere (see 11:18-20; 12:1-4; 15:15-18; 17:14-18) have many elements of prayers by the innocent in the book of Psalms: an invocation of the Lord as just judge, a lament about unjust attacks, an appeal to innocence, and a cry for vindication that often calls for the Lord to pay back in kind those who unjustly attack the petitioner. See for examples Pss 5, 7, 17, and 54, among many others.

verses.zh: 岂可以恶报善呢？他们竟挖坑要害我的性命！求你记念我怎样站在你面前为他们代求，要使你的忿怒向他们转消。
verses.en: Should good be paid back with evil?Yet they are virtually digging a pit to kill me.[NOTE:1] Just remember how I stood before youpleading on their behalf[NOTE:2] to keep you from venting your anger on them.[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “They are plotting to kill me”; Heb “They have dug a pit for my soul.” This is a common metaphor for plotting against someone. See BDB 500 s.v. כָּרָה Qal and for an example see Pss 7:16 (7:15 HT) in its context.
Heb “to speak good concerning them,” which goes back to the concept of “good” being paid back with evil.
Heb “to turn back your anger from them.”sn See Jer 14:7-9, 19-21 and 15:1-4 for the idea.

verses.zh: 故此，愿你将他们的儿女交与饥荒和刀剑；愿他们的妻无子，且作寡妇；又愿他们的男人被死亡所灭，他们的少年人在阵上被刀击杀。
verses.en: So let their children die of starvation.Let them be cut down by the sword.[NOTE:1] Let their wives lose their husbands and children.Let the older men die of disease[NOTE:2] and the younger men die by the sword in battle.
notes: Heb “be poured out to the hand [= power] of the sword.” For this same expression see Ezek 35:5 and Ps 63:10 (63:11 HT). Comparison with those two passages shows that it involved death by violent means, perhaps death in battle.

Heb “be slain by death.” The commentaries are generally agreed that this refers to death by disease or plague as in 15:2. Hence, the reference is to the deadly trio of sword, starvation, and disease, which were often connected with war. See the notes on 15:2.

verses.zh: 你使敌军忽然临到他们的时候，愿人听见哀声从他们的屋内发出；因他们挖坑要捉拿我，暗设网罗要绊我的脚。
verses.en: Let cries of terror be heard in their houseswhen you send bands of raiders unexpectedly to plunder them.[NOTE:1] For they have virtually dug a pit to capture meand have hidden traps for me to step into.
notes: Heb “when you bring marauders in against them.” For the use of the noun translated here “bands of raiders to plunder them,” see 1 Sam 30:3, 15, 23 and BDB 151 s.v. גְּדוּד 1.

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，他们要杀我的那一切计谋，你都知道。不要赦免他们的罪孽，也不要从你面前涂抹他们的罪恶，要叫他们在你面前跌倒；愿你发怒的时候罚办他们。
verses.en: But you, Lord, knowall their plots to kill me.Do not pardon their crimes!Do not ignore their sins as though you had erased them.[NOTE:1] Let them be brought down in defeat before you.Deal with them while you are still angry!”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Do not blot out their sins from before you.” For this anthropomorphic figure that looks at God’s actions as though connected with record books, i.e., a book of wrongdoings to be punished and a book of life for those who are to live, see, e.g., Exod 32:32, 33, Pss 51:1 (51:3 HT); and 69:28 (69:29 HT).
Heb “in the time of your anger.”

"Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: JEREMIAH 18:1-4

1The word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord
saying, 2"Arise and go down to the potter's house, and there I will announce My words to you." 3Then I
went down to the potter's house, and there he was, making something on the wheel. 4But the vessel that he was
making of clay was spoiled in the hand of the potter; so he remade it into another vessel, as it pleased the potter to make.

18:1 See note at Jer. 7:1.

18:2 The potter is imagery for YHWH (cf. Isa. 29:16; 30:14; 41:25; 64:8; Zech. 11:13; Rom. 9:21;
Rev. 2:27). The VERBAL "formed" (BDB 427, KB 428, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)
is often used of YHWH's creative activity (cf. Gen. 2:7,8,19; Isa. 43:1,21; 44:21; 45:9,11,18). YHWH's covenant
people were part of a larger purpose (see SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL
REDEMPTIVE PLAN), but their covenant disobedience caused that plan to be damaged (cf. Ezek. 36:22-36).
Therefore, the potter starts over again to make a new piece on the wheel (cf. Jer. 18:4). The theological question
is "who/what" is the new piece (i.e. restored Judah or all mankind)?

I have come to believe that the events of A.D. 70 (i.e. the Jewish war with Rome, culminating
in the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple) ended the Mosaic covenant. The church has become the new people
of God. This title is no longer national, but "whosoever will" believe in Jesus as the promised Messiah.

I hope if this paragraph shocks you that you will look at my revised verse-by-verse commentary
(www.freebiblecommentary.org) on

- the Olivet Discourse of Jesus (Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 17; 21)

- the "man of lawlessness" passage in 2 Thess. 2

- my new (2024) exegetical commentary on the book of Revelation

18:3

NASB, Peshitta
"on the wheel"

NKJV
"at the wheel"

NRSV, TEV, NJB, REB, JPSOA, NET
"at his wheel"

LXX
"on the stones"

The MT has

- a PREPOSITION

- the DEFINITE ARTICLE

- dual NOUN "stones" (BDB 6)

This literal translation is followed by the LXX. Potters used two stones

- one on which to put the lump of clay

- another to turn with the foot

18:4 The problem was defective clay not a poorly skilled potter! The clay was/is fallen
(cf. Genesis 3), even with all of YHWH's benefits (cf. Rom. 9:4-5).

The JPSOA translation adds "if," which denotes that not all vessels
were "spoiled." But the context suggests YHWH is depicting Judah as a corporate entity.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: JEREMIAH 18:5-12

5Then the word of the Lord came to me saying,
6"Can I not, O house of Israel, deal with you as this potter does?" declares the Lord.
"Behold, like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel. 7At one moment I might speak
concerning a nation or concerning a kingdom to uproot, to pull down, or to destroy it; 8if that nation against which
I have spoken turns from its evil, I will relent concerning the calamity I planned to bring on it. 9Or at another moment I
might speak concerning a nation or concerning a kingdom to build up or to plant it; 10 if it does evil in My sight by
not obeying My voice, then I will think better of the good with which I had promised to bless it. 11So now then, speak to the
men of Judah and against the inhabitants of Jerusalem saying, 'Thus says the Lord, "Behold, I am fashioning
calamity against you and devising a plan against you. Oh turn back, each of you from his evil way, and reform your ways and your deeds."'
12 But they will say, 'It's hopeless! For we are going to follow our own plans, and each of us will act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart.'

18:7 The actions of YHWH are the very actions given to Jeremiah at his call (cf. Jer. 1:10). YHWH
exercises interest and control over all nations (cf. LXX, Deut.32:8; all the judgment chapters are addressed
to them in the prophets).

- to uproot ‒ BDB 684, KB 737, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

- to pull down ‒ BDB 683, KB 736, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

- to destroy ‒ BDB 1, KB 2, Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

The actions of renewal and rebuilding mentioned in Jer. 1:10 (also note Jer. 31:28) are conditionally
stated in Jer. 18:8-9. Faith and faithfulness have consequences, as do idolatry and disobedience (cf. Jer. 18:10). For
a good brief discussion of God changing His mind, see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 209-210, 333-334.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY (OT), III.

18:8,10 "if. . ." There are some unconditional promises based on YHWH's desire to redeem
mankind. However, they are addressed to nations and individuals on conditional bases
(i.e. Jer. 7:3-7; 12:16). This is where the doctrine of "God's Sovereignty" and "Human Freewill" meet!

SPECIAL TOPIC: Predestination (Calvinism) Versus Human Free Will (Arminianism)

SPECIAL TOPIC: Election/Predestination and the Need for a Theological Balance

18:8 "I will relent" This is the VERB "be sorry" (BDB 636, KB 688, Niphal
PERFECT with waw), often translated "repent." It is difficult to speak of YHWH as
"repenting." This is obviously anthropomorphic language (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE). YHWH is willing to change (His actions,
but not His character, cf. Num. 23:19; 1 Sam. 15:29; see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 209-210) based on:

- a person's/nation's change of attitude and actions

- intercessory prayer

There are several places where this VERB is used of YHWH (cf. Gen. 6:6-7;
Exod. 32:14; 1 Sam. 15:11; 2 Sam. 24:16; Ps. 106;45; Jer. 18:7,8; 26:13,19; Amos 7:3,6; Jonah 3:9-4:2,11). However,
the opposite is also stated in Scripture (cf. Num. 23:19; 1 Sam. 15:29; Ps. 132:11; Jer. 4:28; Ezek. 24:14; Mal. 3:6;
James 1:17). YHWH chooses grace over judgment, if humans will only respond in faith and faithfulness. Prophecy (except Messianic) is conditional.

Three good references I trust on this issue are:

- F. F. Bruce, Answers to Questions, pp. 129-130

- Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 70-75

- D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks, pp. 44-47

18:11 YHWH, like the potter, made and destroyed a piece of defective pottery. The VERBAL
(BDB 427, KB 428, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) translated "fashioning" is the same Qal
PARTICIPLE translated "potter" (vv. 2, 3, 4 [twice], 6 [twice], 11). It is also used of God's activity

- in forming Adam (cf. Gen. 2:7,8)

- in forming Jeremiah (Jer. 1:5)

- in forming a nation from Abraham's seed (cf. Isa. 27:11; 43:1,21; 44:21; 45:9,11; 64:8).

▣ "I am fashioning calamity against you and devising a plan against you" The OT asserts the full
sovereignty of YHWH. His control of "all" events (i.e. one causality in the universe) was a theological way of
asserting monotheism. This "one causality" can be seen in 2 Chr. 20:6; Eccl. 7:14; Isa. 14:24-27; 43:13; 45:7;
54:16; Jer. 18:11; Lam. 3:33-38). For a good brief discussion of this see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 305-306. This,
in no way, is meant to assert that YHWH is the source of evil!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

The same VERB (BDB 427, KB 426, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)
is used of a potter fashioning clay in Isa. 29:16; 41:25; Jer. 18:4 [twice], 6 [twice]). It is used in the famous passage
of YHWH's initial creation of human beings in Gen. 2:7,8 and of Jeremiah in the womb in Jer. 1:5.

Here, it refers to YHWH forming, fashioning Israel (cf. Isa. 27:11; 43:1,21; 44:21; 45:9 [twice], 11;
64:7) for His larger purposes of the redemption of all mankind, but they failed!

Notice that true repentance is not only a turning from evil, but a turning to good! Eternal life has observable characteristics.

18:12 This is YHWH's understanding of the unrepentant heart of Judah (cf. Jer. 2:25; 17:1). They will
not, they cannot change (cf. Jer. 13:23). They have passed the time of repentance. They continue to walk in open-eyed
rebellion (cf. Jer. 7:24; 9:13; 13:10; 16:12)!

Or is the cold flowing water from a foreign land ever snatched away?

15For My people have forgotten Me,

They burn incense to worthless gods

And they have stumbled from their ways,

From the ancient paths,

To walk in bypaths,

Not on a highway,

16To make their land a desolation,

An object of perpetual hissing;

And shake his head.

17Like an east wind I will scatter them

Before the enemy;

I will show them My back and not My face

In the day of their calamity.'"

18:13-17 This strophe describes the horrible and unique situation of a nation changing
her god/gods (cf. Jer. 2:9-13). YHWH formed/created them but now they have "forgotten"
(BDB 1013, KB 1489, Qal PERFECT, cf. Jer. 2:32; 3:21; 13:25) Him, the
only true God, the One who brought them into existence, protected them, provided for them,
was personally present with them (i.e. Israel as YHWH's wife imagery)!

How could this happen?

- They burned incense to worthless gods.

- They stumbled from God's clearly revealed way (i.e. ancient paths, cf. Jer. 6:16; Ps. 16:11;
139:24; see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY).

- They walked in bypaths that were not YHWH's path.

What are the consequences of their choices/actions?

- The land of promise will be a desolation (cf. Lev. 26; Deut. 28).

- It will be a sign of shame and scorn (lit. "shake the head," cf. Jer. 48:27).

- They will be scattered (cf. Lev. 26:33; Jer. 9:16; 13:24; 31:10).

- YHWH will show them His back and not His face (this is a revocalization of the MT; see JPSOA footnote).

18:13 "The virgin of Israel" The virgin wife of Israel was a faithless, adulterous wife! See full note at Jer. 46:11.

▣ "a most appalling thing" This phrase is used of a nation changing gods. The
word "appalling" (BDB 1045 III, KB 1619 III) has several forms.

- שׁערור = horrible things, cf. Jer. 5:30; 23:14

- שׁערורי = something horrible, cf. Jer. 18:13; Hosea 6:10

- שׁער = rotten figs, cf. Jer. 29:17

18:14 This verse (a parenthetical statement) is difficult to translate. It obviously
describes that which normally or expectedly occurs. Here apparently, the snow stays on Mt. Hermon
and its melted waters continually flow down. Nature can be predicted with regularity, but not the
seed of Abraham (i.e. Jer. 2:11-13; 8:7; Isa. 1:3)!

18:15 "My people have forgotten Me" This phrase has several implications.

- Israel/Judah have violated their marriage vows with YHWH (i.e. spiritual adultery)

- Israel/Judah have violated YHWH's revelation/law (i.e. covenant disobedience)

This is recurrent and powerful imagery of a broken relationship (cf. Deut. 6:12; 8:11; Ps. 106:21; Isa. 17:10; 51:13;
Jer. 2:32; 3:21; 13:25; Hosea 2:13; 4:6; 8:14; 13:6). The two exiles (i.e. Assyria and Neo-Babylon) and the foretold destruction of
Jerusalem again (cf. Dan. 9:24-27, which became a reality in A.D. 66-70, cf. Matt. 24;
Mark 13; Luke 17; 21; 2 Thess. 2; the book of Revelation).

It must be restated again and again that humans were created in God's image and likeness
for fellowship, not for dependance on self actualization. We need a vital, intimate, personal faith relationship
with our Creator.

▣ "worthless gods" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: EMPTY, VAIN, FALSE, NOTHINGNESS

▣ "Not on a highway" Jer. 18:15 resumes the theme of apostasy from Jer. 18:13. The image
of a special highway is recurrent in Isaiah (i.e. a way to easity and quickly come to YHWH).

- a highway for the exiled Jews to return, Isa. 11:16; 57:14

- a highway for Gentile worshipers to come, Isa. 19:23

- a highway of holiness, Isa. 26:7; 35:8; 43:19; 49:11; 51:10

- a Messianic highway, Isa. 40:3; 42:16

It is possible that this imagery refers to lifestyle faith (i.e. Ps. 1:1-6; Jer. 6:16; 12:16; 31:21).
The ancient path is a way of referring to daily covenant obedience. Biblical faith is

- a Person to know (i.e. "Me")

- truths about that Person's will to believe (i.e. inspired revelation)

- a lifestyle of faithfulness to that revelation (#2)

He settled in His land. They were to be a light to the nations, but they became an object of scorn (i.e. "perpetual

18:17 "the east wind" This wind (BDB 924 CONSTRUCT BDB 870) is imagery for the
seasonal winds that affect Palestine. The east wind (Arabic sirocco) is a hot, strong desert wind that causes destruction
(i.e. Gen. 41:6,23,27; Job 38:24; Ps. 48:7; Isa. 27:8; Hosea 12:2; 13:15; Jonah 4:8).

▣ "I will show them My back and not My face" The MT has "My back and not My face I will show them."
This is an idiom for rejection and broken fellowship. It is opposite of the Aaronic blessing of Num. 6:22-26.

18:20 "Should good be repaid with evil" Apparently this refers to Jeremiah's prayers
("I stood before You") for Judah (cf. Jer. 17:16), but they responded by trying to kill him.

▣ "they have dug a pit for me" This is an allusion to a hunting technique (cf. Ps. 57:6; 119:85). It
may be literal (i.e. they will try to kill him) or figurative (they will try to ruin his reputation, cf. Jer. 18:22, i.e.
his prophecies have not occurred, cf. Deut. 13:1-5).

▣ "how I stood before You" The physical position of Jewish prayer was

- standing

- eyes open

- head up

- hands outstretched and raised

This implies that prayer is a dialogue with God.

18:21-22 Jeremiah tried to present YHWH's word to the people of Judah, but they rejected and ignored this
revelation. His own family (tribe) even attacked him. Jeremiah's prayers "for" Judah changed to his prayers
"against" Judah. This mimicked YHWH's thoughts.

In many ways these calls for judgment reflect the "imprecatory Psalms" (i.e. parts of Psalms 5; 6; 10; 12;
35; 37; 40; 52; 54-59; 69; 70; 79; 83; 94; 109; 129; 137; 139; 140; 143).

These Psalms, as well as the prophetic parallels, are an attempt to arrest people's attention to the
"justice" of God. There is a judgment coming for unrepentant, unbelieving, unfaithful humans. These passages are
designed to shock and redirect wayward humans.

18:23 Is Jeremiah being vindictive? He seems to want justice for Judah's repeated covenant
violations. His own circumstances bothered him but Judah's sin bothered him more! There will be
justice. There will be a day when humans give an account to God for the gift of life
(i.e. Matt. 25:31-46; Rev. 20:11-15). It will be an especially bad day for covenant, informed people (cf. Luke 12:48)!
